new_statements.translation: Thus Abaza stress, which carries an important meaning-distinguishing function, has no fixed place in the word, and words of all possible stress types occur (on the first, second, third etc. syllable of a polysyllabic [lit. 'numerous'] word). [...] Fixed stress. By their stress the words of Abaza divide into two basic types: words with fixed stress and words with mobile stress; the shift of stress takes place when certain auxiliary morphemes, normally lacking a stress of their own (case endings, tense and mood endings, etc.), are attached to the lexical stem.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Free (non-fixed), strongly distinctive dynamic word stress: any syllable of the word may carry it and many word pairs differ only in stress placement (а́ла 'eye' vs ала́ 'dog', а́сра 'beat' vs асра́ 'weave'). Placement is lexically and morphologically determined: closed-monosyllabic stems and polysyllabic stems with non-final stress keep stress fixed under affixation; open-monosyllabic (CV) stems have mobile stress that shifts forward onto stress-accepting suffixes or back onto prefixes (article a-), while a class of suffixes (-la instrumental, -ta, -da, most derivational formants) never accepts stress. In later comparative terms (Dybo 1977/2000/2007, Spruit 1986, Moroz & Kuznetsova 2022) morphemes/syllables are dominant or recessive and stress falls on the first dominant element that is followed by a recessive one or by the word end (all-recessive words: Dybo says final, Moroz & Kuznetsova say initial).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Genko p. 66: long predicative (verbal) complexes may carry two stresses, 'the second weakened' (уыгIасзынхатIд 'you remained for me'); Lomtatidze 2006 p. 112: complex stems and compounds have one main stress, 'sometimes a co-stress of lesser force is possible'. No rhythmic secondary stress rule is given.
new_statements.exceptions: Genko p. 65-66: isolated unmotivated deviations (лы́мхIа 'ear' but лымхIа́ла; та́ба 'pan' but таба́ла); compound and predicative-complex stress 'not reducible to simple formulas'; interrogative -ma takes stress in the Karapago (Kuvinsk) subdialect unlike Tapanta proper and Abkhaz; many polysyllabic loans (революца, бригада) have fixed stress. Phonetically Genko notes Abaza stress involves no noticeable pitch rise or lengthening and is harder to hear than Russian or Abkhaz stress (p. 63); Dybo, Nikolaev & Starostin 1978 claim a high/low tone distinction on the stressed syllable in Tapanta.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level ('udarenie slovesnoe') on citation and inflected forms; Genko separately treats phrase-level 'syntactic' stress (one word of a close-knit phrase made more prominent, others keeping weakened stress) and 'logical' (emphatic) stress, and hiatus resolution merging phrase-mates into one phonetic word.
new_statements.identity_note: Genko 1955 explicitly describes the Tapanta dialect (narechie tapanta; Glottolog tapa1257), the basis of literary Abaza; Klychev & Chkadua 1999 and Lomtatidze 2006 describe literary Abaza (Tapanta-based, with Ashkharywa/ashk1234 notes). Moroz & Kuznetsova's 2022 draft covers Tapanta as spoken in Inzhich-Chukun and Krasnyj Vostok (Gumlokt). Lomtatidze 2006 is the Russian original of the text published in English as Lomtatidze & Klychev 1989 'Abaza' (Hewitt ed.), i.e. the source the earlier scan named as unreachable.

sources.note: 'Stress in Abaza is distinctive (saˈɾa «I» vs. ˈsaɾa «lamb»). Each Abaza morpheme.. can be represented by combination of open syllables with vowel a or ə.. each syllable assigned to one of the accentual classes: dominant or recessive. The main stress rule is formulated in (Spruit 1986: 37-40): stress falls on the first D element followed by R or word boundary, otherwise stress is on the first syllable.' Based on 50 minimal pairs recorded from 13 speakers; unfinished draft.

sources.note: Comparative: Abkhaz, Tapanta (Abaza) and Ubykh preserve the West Caucasian paradigmatic accent system; morphemes are dominant or recessive (-) and 'ударение всегда ставится в конце первой последовательности морфем высшей валентности' (stress at the end of the first sequence of highest-valency morphemes; all-recessive words get final stress). Notes Starostin seemed to detect weak tones in Tapanta; complains Abaza dictionaries omit stress marks although 'роль ударения в абазинском языке неизмеримо выше, чем в русском'.
